Notes:
Title: 30-m Landsat Cropland Mapping of Australia and China on Google Earth Engine

Part: Introduction (about 80 words)
- 2018 study, Teluguntla and colleagues, ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
- Made high-accuracy 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China
- Used Landsat-8, random forest classifier, Google Earth Engine (GEE)
- Results matter, but method is the bigger story
- Shows continent-scale, field-level mapping is practical, repeatable, affordable

Part: Why Australia and China? (about 50 words)
- China: huge population, comparatively small farmland area, fragmented intensively managed plots
- Australia: vast sparsely populated farm regions, large fields, dryland farming, irrigation in particular basins
- If one approach maps both well, good sign it travels to other regions
- That was the study's central bet

Part: Why 30 meters matters (about 100 words)
- Earlier global land cover products used 250 m to 1 km imagery
- One pixel mixes crops, fallow land, trees, roads, buildings
- Small-field places like much of China: cropland extent hard to pin down
- Landsat-8: 30-meter pixels, resolve individual fields in many areas
- Temporal dimension crucial: cropland defined by what it does over time as much as how it looks on one date

Part: The method in brief (about 40 words)
- Time-series imagery: multiple Landsat-8 observations, not one cloud-free scene
- Composited into summaries of seasonal vegetation patterns; cropland's rise and fall in greenness informs classifier

Part: Google Earth Engine as enabler (about 90 words)
- Traditionally: download terabytes, store locally, preprocess, heavy computation on dedicated hardware
- Barrier kept many teams from attempting the work
- Write analysis once, run over huge areas without moving data
- Makes approach scalable: same code for another region with little change, results refreshed as new imagery arrives

Part: Why random forest fits (about 30 words)
- Valuable for large-area mapping: predictable across very different landscapes, easier to scale than per-region recalibration

Part: The method in brief (about 40 words)
- Training and validation samples: cropland/non-cropland reference data, used to train and separately to test
- Independent sets essential for honest accuracy estimate

Part: Strengths and caveats (about 60 words)
- Binary map doesn't say which crops, whether irrigated, or how intensively farmed
- Supervised classification quality depends on quality and spatial coverage of reference samples, costly over large areas
- Cloud cover can limit usable observations in some regions and seasons

Part: Food and water security (about 70 words)
- Cropland footprint helps estimate irrigation demand, pressure on river basins and aquifers, target water management
- Especially relevant: Australia (water allocation constant concern), northern China (serious groundwater depletion)
- Consistent method allows comparisons national datasets with differing definitions and standards often cannot

Notes:
Title: Community Resource Centers for Children in Uganda's Peri-Urban Slums

Part: Intro: Life on Kampala's edges (about 80 words)
- Small children left with slightly older siblings while parents/guardians seek daily work
- Orphans, children of very young mothers may have no reliable adult at all
- Kampala-based organization working in these communities proposes direct response: free, safe, community-run resource centers

Part: The Problem: A Cycle That Repeats Itself (about 130 words)
- Each feeds the next; girl mother too early without support likely raises children in poverty, who face same risks
- Early parenthood: many girls mothers as teenagers, leave school, little info on pregnancy, childbirth, infant care
- Unsafe environments: caregivers working long hours/away, children unsupervised; exposed to traffic, polluted water, abuse, exploitation
- Poor nutrition and health: irregular meals, limited clinic access; malnutrition, preventable illness, affects development for life
- Proposal's starting idea: break the cycle at several points at once

Part: For Mothers and Guardians (about 90 words)
- Caregivers treated as partners, not just service users
- Safe-motherhood education: prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, newborn care; esp. young and first-time mothers
- Skills training: vocational and small-business skills for stable income, independence
- Teenage girl seeing real alternative to early motherhood can turn the cycle's direction

Part: For Children (about 50 words)
- Basic health care: growth monitoring, immunization follow-up, deworming, first aid, referrals to clinics/hospitals
- For orphans and most fragile households, center may be the one consistent, caring place in their day

Part: Community Ownership: Built With, Not For (about 60 words)
- What sets proposal apart: insistence on community ownership; not outside institutions dropped in, meant to belong to neighborhood
- Local staffing and volunteering: caregivers/volunteers from surrounding area where possible; creates jobs, builds trust

Part: Partner Networks: No Center Stands Alone (about 30 words)
- Modest neighborhood center becomes gateway to wider web of support

Part: Community Ownership: Built With, Not For (about 30 words)
- Also about sustainability: programs dependent on outside funding and staff tend to fade when support ends; community-owned ones far more likely to last

Title: The Border Collie: From Drover's Dog to Herding Prodigy

Part: Opening: Herding Miracle (about 60 words)
- Dog drops low, locks eyes on flock, quiet intensity like chess player three moves ahead
- No barking, no chaos; stare, slow arc around sheep, flock goes exactly where asked

Part: The Eye, the Stalk, the Brain (about 110 words)
- These = modified predatory sequence of wolves and other canids: orient, eye, stalk, chase
- In border collies grab-and-kill end largely bred out; early steps run with extraordinary refinement
- The eye: intense fixed stare pressuring livestock without contact
- The stalk: low deliberate approach, moves sheep by presence not force
- Responsiveness: unusual willingness to take handler direction, even at distance

Part: Rugged Beginnings on the Border (about 50 words)
- Selection brutally practical; not breeding for ribbons, breeding a dog to bring flock home
- Dogs that thought independently, endured bad weather, read animal movement earned keep and passed on traits

Part: Adam Telfer and Foundation (about 60 words)
- Adam Telfer, Northumberland shepherd, 19th century; often credited with consolidating the type via deliberate crossbreeding, strengthening wanted working qualities
- Telfer's contribution not a look but fixing working traits so they reappear each generation

Part: Working Over Looks (about 110 words)
- Heart of breed's identity: unlike show-ring-standard breeds, shaped by working-over-looks ethos; herded = bred, couldn't = appearance didn't save it
- Black and white classic; merles, reds, tricolors and others too; variety = fingerprint of breeders caring about ability above all
- Sheepdog trials, begun 19th century, still popular; reinforced focus; let shepherds compare dogs side by side, rewarding calm, efficient stock movement under pressure

Part: The Flip Side: Demanding Temperament (about 120 words)
- Admiration needs realism; traits brilliant in pasture can be difficult in typical home
- Behaviorist Patricia McConnell, writes on herding breeds, herded with her own border collies: dogs bred to work, drive doesn't switch off in a house
- Dog built to control moving things may fixate on cars, bicycles, joggers, children
- Practical signs: nipping heels or herding family, esp. kids
- Dog built to think all day invents own jobs if none given; you may not like them

Part: Is It Right for You? (about 30 words)
- Needs real mental work: training, puzzles, structured games, dog sports (agility, flyball), ideally actual herding

Part: A Breed Made by Work (about 30 words)
- Give it a job and it astonishes; leave it without one and it finds its own

Notes:
Title: The Atholl Memorial Fountain and the Atholl Family in Dunkeld

Part: A fountain for a gift of water (about 50 words)
- Fountain dates from 1866; commemorates George Murray, 6th Duke of Atholl, died 1864
- His great public service: piped water to the town

Part: A landmark that still serves (about 30 words)
- Few stop to think monument inspired by something as ordinary as turning on a tap

Part: A fountain for a gift of water (about 110 words)
- Previously wells, springs, river; water carried by hand; quality uncertain
- Reliable piped supply a major Victorian improvement; less drudgery, less disease risk
- Fitting that townspeople chose a fountain, not a statue on a plinth
- Structure itself delivers water, tying memorial to benefit celebrated
- Reminder that water to homes was a gift of the estate

Part: The Murrays and Dunkeld (about 90 words)
- Murrays held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries; rose through Scottish nobility; Duke of Atholl title created 1703
- Seat at Blair Castle, to the north; Dunkeld always within their orbit
- After the Reformation cathedral partly ruined; family influence grew as old church structures lost authority
- Much land and property around cathedral came under family control

Part: Fire, rebuilding, planned town (about 60 words)
- 1689, after Battle of Killiecrankie: fierce fight between Jacobite Highlanders and Cameronian regiment; much of town burned
- Estate shaped street layout, cathedral setting, wider landscape
- "Little Houses": row of small sturdy cottages, restored in twentieth century by National Trust for Scotland; hint at modest vernacular architecture of post-fire town

Part: Bridge, cathedral and woodland (about 140 words)
- Estate stewardship of cathedral grounds helped preserve site giving Dunkeld age and dignity
- Telford's bridge over Tay, completed 1809, when 4th Duke was powerful in district
- Replaced ferries; gave lasting grand link to the south
- 4th Duke remembered for passion for trees: "Planter Duke"
- Planted vast numbers of larches and other conifers across Atholl lands; Dunkeld woodlands still bear mark
- Plantations transformed look of hills, part of area's identity, still draw walkers and visitors

Notes:
Title: Five Simple, Surprising Ways to Help Save the Planet

Part: 2. Commercial Car Wash (about 140 words)
- Surprising: washing at home feels thrifty and harmless but often isn't good for environment
- Many areas: storm drains carry runoff untreated to streams, rivers, lakes
- Driveway wash: water, soap, brake dust, oil, road grime run into storm drain
- Running garden hose can use more water than expected
- Environmental: commercial washes generally required to send wastewater to treatment, not storm drains; many use high-pressure, low-volume equipment and water reclamation, much less fresh water per car
- Swap: professional car wash, ideally one that recycles water

Part: 4. Local, Seasonal Food (about 140 words)
- Honest caveat: transportation usually smaller share of food's footprint than how it's produced
- Environmental: fresher produce lasts longer at home, less food waste; food waste among biggest household contributors to greenhouse gas emissions
- Still, local/seasonal often means less packaging, less refrigerated storage, less spoilage before reaching you; supports local farms
- Financial: in-season produce often cheaper because plentiful; longer-lasting food means fewer wasted dollars
- Tip: start with one weekly item (eggs, apples, tomatoes in summer) bought locally; build from there

Part: 1. Rechargeable Batteries (about 80 words)
- Modern "low self-discharge" versions hold charge for months in drawer; fine for low-drain devices
- Financial: higher upfront cost, often pays for itself after a handful of charges in frequently used devices; then recharges cost pennies
- Environmental: one rechargeable reused hundreds of times, replaces pile of disposables

Part: 5. Reusable Cleaning Supplies (about 60 words)
- Financial: pack of microfiber cloths costs about same as a few rolls of paper towels, lasts years; concentrates much cheaper per use than ready-to-use bottles
- Tip: small basket for used cloths under sink, launder with regular wash; keep paper towels for truly messy jobs; goal is to cut back, not be perfect

Notes:
Title: How Often to Check Blood Pressure at Home

Part: Introduction (about 50 words)
- Single doctor's-office reading is only a snapshot
- Home monitoring shows bigger picture: ordinary days, away from clinic stress

Part: How Often Should You Measure? (about 240 words)
- Diagnosed with high BP or doctor asked: readings for about seven days before appointment or after medication change
- Twice a day, morning and evening; two readings each time, one minute apart
- Many guidelines: discard first day's results, average the rest
- Well controlled: once stable, cut back; a few times a week, or one-week round every month or so; clinician advises
- Proactive, no diagnosis: especially over 40 or with risk factors (family history, diabetes, excess weight, kidney disease), occasional checks help
- Reasonable: a week of readings every few months, or whenever a clinic reading is high
- More not always better: constant checking fuels anxiety, overreacting to normal fluctuations
- BP naturally rises and falls through day; patterns matter more than single readings

Part: When During the Day (about 110 words)
- Consistency is key: same times each day so readings comparable
- Morning: within an hour of waking, after bathroom, before eating, coffee, exercise, or BP medication
- Morning is when BP tends to surge; surge linked to cardiovascular events, so readings especially valuable
- Avoid measuring after caffeine, smoking, exercise, alcohol; wait at least 30 minutes

Part: The Right Technique (about 280 words)
- Even a good device misleads if setup wrong; small errors can add 10 points or more
- 4. Cuff size: one of most overlooked errors; too small reads high, too large can read low
- Check: measure middle of upper arm, compare to size range on cuff or manual; standard cuff usually included, other sizes sold separately
- Cuff on bare skin, not over clothing; roll up sleeve if not loose but avoid tourniquet effect
- Arm below heart level = falsely high; above = falsely low
- Crossing legs or dangling feet can noticeably raise BP
- 1. Rest first: sit quietly at least five minutes; no talking, phone scrolling, stressful viewing; empty bladder (full bladder raises reading)
- 5. Validated upper-arm monitor: automatic upper-arm generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices
- Choose clinically validated; consider bringing to appointment to compare with clinic equipment
- Same arm each time, ideally the higher-reading one, as doctor may advise

Part: Making Sense of Numbers (about 140 words)
- Home average 130/80 or higher: elevated enough to discuss with doctor; targets vary by individual
- Don't diagnose or adjust medication yourself; bring log to appointment so clinician sees full pattern
- Urgent attention if 180/120 or higher, especially with chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, weakness, difficulty speaking
- Very high reading without symptoms: rest five minutes, remeasure; if still that high, contact doctor promptly

Notes:
Title: Cyber Torts, Strict Liability, and Products Liability in Business Law

Part: Tort vs. Contract Law (about 90 words)
- Contract: parties create own obligations by agreement
- Tort: law imposes duty (act reasonably, don't deliberately harm, don't make false reputation-damaging statements)
- Business relevance: exposure needs no signed document
- Examples: delivery driver crash, website publishing false accusation, manufacturer's product injuring bystander

Part: Intentional vs. Unintentional Torts (about 60 words)
- Distinction matters: intentional wrongdoing can bring punitive damages; insurance often excludes intentional acts, covers negligence
- Intentional torts: deliberate act causes harm; need intend only the act, not full extent of damage
- Negligence needs four elements: duty of care, breach, causation, damages

Part: Cyber Torts (about 40 words)
- Business exposure: as perpetrators (rarely); more often as data custodians
- Failure to protect sensitive data with reasonable safeguards: negligence claims after breach, plus regulatory enforcement, statutory penalties

Part: Intentional vs. Unintentional Torts (about 30 words)
- Examples: store not cleaning spill after warning; company neglecting basic data security; no intent to hurt

Part: Cyber Torts (about 90 words)
- Written = libel, spoken = slander; online posts typically libel
- Businesses careful about statements on competitors, former employees, and responses to negative reviews
- US wrinkle: Section 230 of Communications Decency Act generally shields platforms from liability for user content
- Author of defamatory statement still responsible; hosting platform usually not

Part: Strict Liability (about 40 words)
- Strict liability: liable for harm even with all possible care; no negligence need be proven
- Reasoning: whoever chooses hazardous activity and profits should bear the cost of harm

Part: Products Liability (about 90 words)
- Strict liability showing: product defective, defect existed when it left defendant's control, defect caused injury
- Three defect types: manufacturing (departs from intended design)
- Design defects (design unreasonably dangerous)
- Failure to warn (inadequate instructions or warnings about known risks)
- Liability extends through distribution chain: retailers, wholesalers may be named with manufacturers

Part: Common Defenses (about 60 words)
- Strict liability is not automatic liability; defenses vary by state
- Product misuse: not reasonably foreseeable use
- Product alteration or modification after leaving defendant's hands
- Compliance with government standards: may help, often not a complete shield

Notes:
Title: Texas Maternal Mortality Task Force: Extension and Maternal Health Crisis

Part: Introduction (about 80 words)
- Texas asking whether to keep studying why mothers die; answer yes, but wrong place to stop
- Extension necessary, not enough; panel that diagnoses can't cure; that's Legislature's job
- Extension on special session agenda; should pass quickly

Part: Why task force must continue (about 60 words)
- Brings together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, public health experts to review deaths case by case
- Reveals e.g. death labeled "cardiac arrest" followed weeks of untreated hypertension; overdose followed lost treatment access

Part: A crisis that drew national attention (about 70 words)
- Later reviews: data and reporting errors, incl. how pregnancy recorded on death certificates, inflated some figures
- Data problems don't erase reality: mothers still dying of often preventable causes; deaths fall hardest on same women repeatedly

Part: Why task force must continue (about 30 words)
- Review can't be rebuilt quickly if lapses; expiry mid-crisis, while data being corrected, indefensible

Part: Who is dying, and why (about 220 words)
- Early analysis: Black women about one in nine births, nearly three in ten maternal deaths
- Income and education don't explain gap away; researchers cite access to care, untreated chronic conditions like hypertension before pregnancy, how patients are heard or not when reporting symptoms
- Coverage cliff: Texas Medicaid covers about half of births
- Pregnancy Medicaid ends roughly 60 days after delivery for many low-income mothers
- Task force: large share of deaths occur after window closes; cardiac conditions, overdoses, suicide
- Overdose: one of leading causes of maternal death in Texas, often well after delivery
- Women stable in pregnancy can lose access to substance use treatment and mental health care after baby arrives
- Texas didn't expand Medicaid; parent income limits among strictest in country; mothers go from coverage to none just as risks turn deadly

Part: Studying is not the same as solving (about 40 words)
- Extend postpartum coverage: continuous coverage full year, not two months; most postpartum deaths fall in gap

Part: The real test (about 70 words)
- Extension is easy vote; lawmakers should cast it
- Harder test: acting on what task force says
- Funding study but not preventive care = choosing to document a tragedy rather than end it

Notes:
Title: Seven Words: Gibran's Challenge and a Personal Lexicon

Part: Intro: the challenge and rule (about 130 words)
- Thought experiment in writings attributed to Khalil Gibran: language reduced to seven words
- Rule: not most beautiful or useful, but words that cannot be replaced by anything else
- Trusts bodies and actions, but they only hint at some things; those words are kept

Part: What the Seven Words Teach (about 30 words)
- All live between people: trust, risk, promise, where pointing isn't enough

Part: Love (about 80 words)
- Actions ambiguous: duty, habit, guilt all look like love
- Saying it removes ambiguity; a risk, since named and can't hide behind implication
- Keeps word because it makes the actions mean something

Part: Forgive (about 90 words)
- Apology can be mimed with bowed head; forgiveness can't be performed in silence, since silence is what resentment looks like
- Wrongdoer often waits years for a releasing sentence; speaker is released too
- A hug might mean anything; 'I forgive you' means one thing

Part: Friend (about 80 words)
- The word is a promotion: acquaintances become friends when one says 'you're my friend'; naming changes the relationship
- First time introduced as 'my friend' felt large; no action could confer that status; it had to be said

Part: Believe / Trust (about 40 words)
- Writer received both in low moments; a quiet 'I believe in you' held longer than any act of rescue

Part: Always (about 60 words)
- Needed because actions happen only in the present; a kind gesture today says nothing of tomorrow
- Only a word reaches forward: 'this is not just for now'; may not always be true, but willingness to say and mean it is deeply human

Notes:
Title: Body Language as the Silent Driver of Conversation

Part: Intro: Mehrabian Myth (about 60 words)
- Actual measure was narrow: how people judged feelings and attitudes when words clashed with tone or expression
- He never claimed 93% of all meaning is outside language; can't follow tax law lecture by watching hands
- When words and body disagree, people believe the body

Part: Why the Body Gets the Final Vote (about 40 words)
- Two channels at once: verbal carries content (facts, requests, opinions); nonverbal carries relationship
- Examples: sincere apology while scrolling phone lands as insult; tough feedback with steady, open attention can land as care

Part: Honesty First: Alignment (about 90 words)
- Governing principle: use body language to express what is true, not manufacture what isn't
- People spot incongruence: smile not reaching eyes, eye contact like a stare-down; they feel it even unnamed, trust erodes
- Wanting to listen but posture says 'I'm in a hurry': adjusting is not manipulation, lets intention through
- Pretending interest when none: no posture will save you, and shouldn't

Part: Posture: Frame of Conversation (about 30 words)
- De-escalating tension: lower physical intensity; sit if they sit; angle to side, not face-to-face; drop shoulders; standing over someone in disagreement reads as dominance even unintended

Part: Eye Contact: Most Intimate Signal (about 30 words)
- Emotional or vulnerable moments: side-by-side (walking, driving) eases hard topics by reducing eye contact; looking away can be kind

Part: Gestures: Making Meaning Visible (about 30 words)
- Pointing, chopping, finger-jabbing escalate conflict fast; soften if aiming for resolution

Part: Posture: Frame of Conversation (about 30 words)
- Confidence or authority: upright, weight balanced, unhurried movement; confidence is stillness, not taking up space; no fidgeting or retreating

Part: Read the Room, Including Yourself (about 30 words)
- They lean back when you lean in: give space; they mirror relaxed posture: connection growing

Part: Eye Contact: Most Intimate Signal (about 30 words)
- Cultural differences: norms vary widely; sustained gaze can read as disrespect

Part: Read the Room, Including Yourself (about 40 words)
- Also notice own body: clenched jaw before meeting, arms crossing at certain topic are signals to heed
- Sometimes honest adjustment is to understanding of how you feel, not posture

Title: Limitations of GDP as a Measure of Economic Well-Being

Part: Quick Review (about 30 words)
- Key takeaway: GDP excellent for total market output, poor stand-alone well-being measure; real GDP per capita preferred for comparing living standards but interpret with caution

Part: Limitation 1: Population Differences (about 50 words)
- A has four times B's total output
- Per person: A $10,000 vs B $50,000; B's average resident has far more goods and services

Part: Why GDP Per Capita Is Better (about 50 words)
- If real GDP grows 3 percent but population 4 percent, output per person falls; living standards likely declining on average
- PPP adjustments often used for price-level differences across countries

Part: Limitation 2: Income Inequality (about 70 words)
- Identical GDP per capita can mean very different living conditions: broad vs concentrated income
- Example: top 1 percent of households earns half of all income; per capita looks healthy, typical household may struggle
- Rising GDP doesn't guarantee gains reach everyone; growth can concentrate among high earners while median incomes stagnate

Part: Limitation 4: Shadow Economy (about 60 words)
- Non-market production also excluded: unpaid housework, childcare, volunteer work; real value but no market transaction
- Shadow economy size varies widely; in some developing countries informal activity is large share of output, so official GDP can substantially understate activity and make cross-country comparisons less accurate

Part: Limitation 3: Environmental Costs (about 100 words)
- Polluting factory adds to GDP; lost water quality and health costs not subtracted
- Disaster cleanup can increase GDP since repair/remediation spending counts as production
- Link to negative externalities: costs on third parties not in market prices; GDP built from market transactions so misses them
- Country can post strong growth while degrading natural capital future generations need

Notes:
Title: Seaweed Supplements: Iodine Risks and Microalgae Promise

Part: Intro (about 40 words)
- Wrong form and dose can push iodine high enough to disrupt the thyroid it's marketed to help
- Sold as dried snacks, powdered "sea greens," kelp tablets, capsules; claims of thyroid support, detox, metabolic balance

Part: Why Iodine Matters, and Why More Isn't Better (about 150 words)
- Needs are tiny: adults ~150 µg/day; pregnancy ~220 µg; breastfeeding ~290 µg
- Upper limits modest: US adult tolerable upper intake 1,100 µg/day; European authorities lower, 600 µg/day
- Wolff–Chaikoff effect: thyroid's built-in brake temporarily slows hormone production during iodine surges
- Most healthy people adapt and return to normal; in others brake fails or overcorrects
- Excess iodine can trigger hypothyroidism, esp. with autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's)
- Or hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow phenomenon), likelier with nodular goiter or long-standing deficiency
- Or newborn thyroid problems when mothers take high-iodine supplements in pregnancy or breastfeeding

Part: The Problem With Seaweed Supplements (about 170 words)
- 1 g dried kombu can contain over a thousand µg iodine; some samples several times that; one small pinch can exceed a day's upper limit
- 1. Variability: iodine differs by species, harvest location, season, processing; kelp product testing repeatedly finds levels differing substantially from labels, sometimes by large margins
- 2. Concentration: powders and tablets make it easy to consume large amounts of dried seaweed unnoticed
- 3. Stacking: kelp capsule, "thyroid support" blend, iodine multivitamin, iodized salt; total never added up
- 4. Marketing: products for fatigue, weight loss, "sluggish thyroid" attract people most likely to have conditions iodine excess worsens
- Many case reports of thyroid dysfunction tied to kelp supplements and seaweed products, in adults and in infants exposed in pregnancy or via breast milk
- Be wary of products not stating iodine per serving in micrograms

Part: But Doesn't Japan Eat Seaweed? (about 200 words)
- Japan has one of highest iodine intakes, mostly from seaweed; estimates vary widely, many one to several milligrams/day, well above Western upper limits
- Yet no thyroid crisis
- Factor: lifelong adaptation; thyroids of people exposed from childhood may regulate better than those suddenly starting a concentrated supplement
- Factor: food, not pills; eaten in meals, varied types and amounts; nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu
- Factor: preparation; kombu used for dashi broth then discarded or eaten in small amounts; soaking and boiling remove substantial share of iodine, though some goes into broth
- Factor: variability; intake swings day to day, not steady high supplement-like dose
- Japan's record not spotless: iodine-related hypothyroidism documented, esp. heavy kombu consumers; clinicians often advise limiting seaweed with certain thyroid conditions
- Tradition shows high iodine can be tolerated in context; doesn't show a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult raised on low-iodine diet

Notes:
Title: Types of Financial Bubbles and Their Impact on the Stock Market

Part: What Is a Financial Bubble? (about 50 words)
- Bubble: asset price rises far beyond what underlying value justifies
- Prices climb on expectation of more climbing, not more earnings, income or usefulness
- Buyers run out, confidence cracks, prices fall fast; sudden fall = the "burst"

Part: 5. Credit Bubbles (about 60 words)
- Impact: especially dangerous because debt magnifies losses
- Prices fall, borrowers can't repay, lenders pull back, forced selling pushes prices lower
- Money flows into assets, lifting prices, encouraging more borrowing

Part: 1. Market Bubbles (about 50 words)
- Impact: damage rarely contained; falling home values 2007-2008 hit banks, builders, insurers, dragged wider market down sharply
- Stocks tied directly to bubble often fall hardest, but unrelated companies also pulled lower as investors sell whatever they can

Part: 5. Credit Bubbles (about 30 words)
- Defining example: 2008 financial crisis; bank stocks collapsed, credit froze, S&P 500 fell more than 50% from 2007 peak to March 2009 low

Part: 3. Stock Market Bubbles (about 60 words)
- Textbook case: dot-com bubble, late 1990s; money poured into internet firms, many with no profits, sometimes barely a business plan
- Nasdaq peaked March 2000, lost roughly three-quarters of value over next couple of years
- Recovery can take years; Nasdaq didn't regain 2000 peak until 2015

Part: 4. Economic Bubbles (about 40 words)
- Classic case: Japan, late 1980s; soaring stock and real estate prices made country feel invincible; both collapsed early 1990s; economy stagnated for years
- Nikkei peaked end of 1989, didn't return to that level for more than 30 years

Part: 3. Stock Market Bubbles (about 30 words)
- Beginners hurt by buying near top after story is popular

Part: Warning Signs to Watch For (about 110 words)
- No one can time a crash perfectly; bubbles can inflate longer than seems rational; patterns still recur
- Prices far above fundamentals: compare valuations like price-to-earnings ratio with historical averages; extremely high deserves skepticism
- Easy credit: low lending standards, heavy borrowing, leverage amplify bubble
- Weak or nonexistent profits: wary of valuations based on promises not results
- Fear of missing out: if main reason to buy is rising prices, pause

Part: How New Investors Can Protect Themselves (about 30 words)
- Avoid leverage while learning
- Keep emergency fund to avoid forced selling in downturn

Title: Brain Immune Response in Neuronopathic Gaucher Disease Against Viral Infection

Part: Introduction (about 40 words)
- Brain immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make mouse brains more resistant to Sindbis virus
- Preliminary, animals not people

Part: A Quick Primer on Gaucher Disease (about 40 words)
- Enzyme faulty: lipid builds up inside cells
- Types 2 and 3: neuronopathic; glucocerebroside accumulates in nerve cells, neurological damage

Part: The Interferon Connection (about 110 words)
- In neuronopathic Gaucher, pathway seems on without infection; lipid buildup and cellular stress trigger chronic low-level alarm
- Switch on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes; nearby cells enter 'antiviral state'
- Persistent inflammation usually thought to drive neuronal damage and progression
- New study asks: if antiviral defenses primed, what happens with a real virus?

Part: Testing With Sindbis Virus (about 80 words)
- In mice infects neurons, causes encephalitis; useful for studying brain defense
- Compared Gaucher-model mice with controls, both exposed to virus
- Protection linked to pre-existing type I interferon response; ongoing immune activation gave a head start

Part: Why This Matters (about 150 words)
- Double-edged inflammation: neuroinflammation often treated only as problem to suppress; same processes can protect; future therapies targeting interferon pathway in Gaucher may need to weigh both sides
- GBA variants significant genetic risk factor for Parkinson's; carrier rates elevated in some populations, incl. Ashkenazi Jews
- Why do some disease variants stay common? Classic explanation: one copy may give advantage; best-known example sickle cell trait and malaria protection
- Authors call for work on whether Gaucher patients, possibly GBA carriers, have some protection against certain viral infections; open question, not conclusion

Part: Important Caveats (about 60 words)
- Disease models are not carriers: mice modeled full neuronopathic disease; carriers have far milder or no biochemical brain changes; similar priming unknown
- One virus: Sindbis resistance doesn't imply resistance to others; some infections might be worsened by chronically activated immune system

Part: The Bottom Line (about 30 words)
- Future work in human cells, patient populations, carriers needed

Notes:
Title: Historical and Contemporary Debates on the Definition of Marriage

Part: Introduction (about 60 words)
- defenders of 'the traditional definition' imagine single stable arrangement handed down unchanged
- historical record messier

Part: Marriage as a Practical Bargain (about 110 words)
- no priest or religious ceremony needed; consent and intention to live as husband and wife = affectio maritalis
- divorce comparatively easy; rested on continuing consent not sacred bond; ended when consent ended
- romance not expected as foundation; affection could grow; love a pleasant bonus, not requirement
- point: institution never primarily about romantic fulfillment; for most of history an economic and political technology

Part: The Church Takes the Wheel (about 100 words)
- 12th-13th centuries: marriage formally one of seven sacraments
- Fourth Lateran Council, 1215, tightened rules incl. public announcement of intended marriages; curb secret unions, clarify who was wed
- divorce far harder; lifelong union of one man and one woman fixed in Western law and culture
- after Reformation Protestants rejected sacrament but still saw divinely ordained institution; civil governments inherited Church definitions

Part: From Sacrament to Civil Right (about 80 words)
- modern era loosened Church's grip: civil marriage statutes, secular courts, no-fault divorce; marriage recast as legal status run by state
- culture shifted to marrying for love; former side benefit became central justification
- crucial to current debate: if marriage = loving committed partnership of two adults, limiting to opposite-sex couples becomes pressing question

Part: The Case for the Traditional Definition (about 60 words)
- author finds caution argument most respectable, but weakened since marriage already redefined repeatedly (end of arranged unions, no-fault divorce)
- procreative argument: marriage unites the two kinds of people who can create children; gives children mother and father

Part: The Case for Equality and Love (about 30 words)
- childless or infertile couples marry without legitimacy questioned

Part: The Case for the Traditional Definition (about 30 words)
- religious argument: marriage sacred, defined by faith; changing it alters something never the state's to change

Part: The Case for Equality and Love (about 100 words)
- same-sex marriage advocates: state gives legal benefits (inheritance, hospital visitation, tax treatment, parental rights, immigration status); denying some couples = unequal treatment; marriage a civil right
- love-based model most already hold: if adults marry for love and shared life, partners' gender irrelevant to modern purpose
- society celebrating marriage for love can hardly justify excluding people who love differently

Notes:
Title: How Metacognition Closes the Gap Between Perceived and Actual Test Preparedness

Part: Opening: Recognizing vs Producing (about 60 words)
- Common student experience: walk into exam feeling ready after hours with notes; within minutes can't answer questions
- Recognized the material but couldn't produce it
- Not a failure of effort but of calibration: match between how prepared you feel and how prepared you are

Part: Illusion of Mastery (about 90 words)
- Rereading makes material familiar; familiarity creates fluency, sense of ease in processing; brain mistakes fluency for mastery
- Recognition vs recall are different skills; exams usually demand recall
- 2013 review by John Dunlosky and colleagues rated both 'low utility' for long-term learning
- Highlighting: coloring a sentence yellow shows you noticed it was important, not that you can explain, apply, or remember it next week

Part: 1. Self-Quizzing Over Rereading (about 100 words)
- 2008 study, Jeffrey Karpicke and Henry Roediger: repeated self-testers remembered far more a week later than repeated restudiers
- Does two jobs: strengthens memory and gives honest feedback
- Example: explain causes of World War I from memory, stall after second point; find gap now, not on test day
- Forms: flashcards answered before flipping, blank-page 'brain dumps', practice problems without notes, explaining a concept aloud to a friend

Part: 3. Classroom Questioning (about 30 words)
- 'Does everyone understand?' fails because students who don't understand often don't know it

Part: 2. Pre-Exam Reflection Surveys (about 120 words)
- Instructors use short surveys before and after exams; Carnegie Mellon's 'exam wrappers', developed by Marsha Lovett, a well-known version
- Before test: hours studied and methods used; topics most and least confident about; predicted score
- Comparison is the point; example: predicted 90, earned 72, concrete evidence readiness sense was off
- Repeated over a semester, students learn which confidence feelings to trust and which study habits paid off

Part: 4. Growth Mindset Framing (about 50 words)
- Strategies fail if students avoid them; self-testing is uncomfortable because it exposes what you don't know
- Robert and Elizabeth Bjork: 'desirable difficulties', challenges harder in the moment but produce stronger learning

Part: Bringing It Together (about 50 words)
- Simple rule: if a study method feels easy, be suspicious of it
- Goal isn't to feel ready but to test whether you are, before the exam does it for you
